complexity.notes: Correct and quite elegant, but the merge step re-builds every list at every ancestor, which is where the extra log factor (quadratic on skewed trees) comes from. A better O(n) approach for every tree shape exists: ||a single iterative BFS with a collections.deque, popping each level's nodes and appending children||. Also note the generalized skewed case would need recursion depth n, risking RecursionError where an iterative version would not.
complexity.summary: Recursive divide-and-conquer: it computes the level-order lists of both subtrees, then merges them level by level (concatenating same-depth sublists, left before right) and prepends the root's level. Every level list is re-copied at each ancestor, so total work is the sum of all subtree sizes — O(n log n) on the complete tree here, O(n^2) on a skewed one.
